reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: An epiphrenic diverticulum is a pulsion (false) diverticulum of the distal oesophagus, typically within the terminal few centimetres above the diaphragm, and is almost always associated with an underlying oesophageal motility disorder.

Achalasia, distal oesophageal spasm, hypercontractile (jackhammer) oesophagus and other outflow-obstruction disorders raise intraluminal pressure and drive mucosal herniation, so manometry is essential in the work-up.

Typical symptoms are dysphagia, regurgitation of retained and sometimes fermented food, nocturnal aspiration, chest pain and halitosis, though many diverticula are asymptomatic and found incidentally.
Barium swallow best demonstrates the sac and any associated motility abnormality; endoscopy is needed to exclude malignancy within the diverticulum.
Because the diverticulum is a consequence of the motility disorder, effective surgery must address the distal obstruction, usually by adding a myotomy to any diverticulectomy.
Surgical repair combines diverticulectomy (or diverticulopexy), an extended myotomy across the lower oesophageal sphincter and often a partial fundoplication to prevent reflux.
The staple line after diverticulectomy is prone to leak if a distal myotomy is not performed, because unrelieved outflow resistance keeps intraluminal pressure high.
Rare but important complications include carcinoma arising within a long-standing diverticulum, so persistent or atypical symptoms warrant careful endoscopic assessment.
reference.pathophysiology: An epiphrenic diverticulum is a herniation of mucosa and submucosa through the muscular layers of the distal oesophagus, classifying it as a pulsion (false) diverticulum. It develops because a functional or mechanical outflow obstruction at the oesophagogastric junction, most often an underlying motility disorder such as achalasia, distal oesophageal spasm or a hypercontractile oesophagus, generates sustained high intraluminal pressure during swallowing against a poorly relaxing or spastic segment. This pressure forces the mucosa outward at a point of relative muscular weakness just above the diaphragm. Retention of food and secretions within the sac produces stasis symptoms, regurgitation and aspiration risk, and chronic inflammation of the retained material can rarely predispose to malignant change. Because the pressure gradient is the driving force, the diverticulum will tend to recur or the repair to leak unless the distal obstruction is relieved.
additionalDifferentials: distal oesophageal spasm or hypercontractile oesophagus
peptic or malignant distal oesophageal stricture
additionalInvestigations: barium swallow to delineate the sac, its neck and associated dysmotility
high-resolution oesophageal manometry to identify the underlying motility disorder
upper gastrointestinal endoscopy to exclude malignancy and mucosal disease within the sac
computed tomography of the chest to define mediastinal anatomy before surgery
ambulatory pH or reflux monitoring where gastro-oesophageal reflux is suspected
timed barium oesophagogram to assess emptying if achalasia is present
redFlags: progressive dysphagia with significant weight loss suggesting malignancy
recurrent aspiration pneumonia or nocturnal choking
haematemesis or evidence of ulceration within the sac
chest pain with fever or sepsis suggesting perforation
a mass or filling defect within the diverticulum on imaging
reference.prognosis: Asymptomatic small diverticula can be observed with a good prognosis, whereas symptomatic lesions treated with combined diverticulectomy and myotomy generally do well, provided the underlying motility disorder is addressed. Staple-line leak and recurrence are the main risks when the distal obstruction is not relieved.
pitfalls: Performing diverticulectomy without an accompanying myotomy, leading to staple-line leak or recurrence.
Failing to perform manometry and missing the causative motility disorder.
Overlooking a carcinoma developing within a long-standing diverticulum.
Attributing symptoms solely to the sac size when the motility disorder is the true driver.
Omitting an antireflux procedure after myotomy and producing troublesome reflux.
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease, current edition
Shackelford's Surgery of the Alimentary Tract, current edition
management: Observe small asymptomatic diverticula, as they carry a good prognosis without intervention

Offer definitive surgery for symptomatic disease combining diverticulectomy or diverticulopexy with an extended myotomy across the lower oesophageal sphincter and usually a partial fundoplication, so the underlying obstruction is corrected
Treat the causative motility disorder directly, for example achalasia by Heller myotomy or per-oral endoscopic myotomy, since the diverticulum is a consequence of dysmotility
Reduce regurgitation and aspiration with dietary modification, thorough chewing, an upright posture after meals and avoidance of late-night eating
Exclude malignancy within the sac by endoscopy before intervention and maintain surveillance
Monitor postoperatively for staple-line leak and recurrence, and refer to an upper gastrointestinal surgical service
